newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Balkan unrest underlines lack of Western strategy.
newsitem.headline: Balkan unrest underlines lack of Western strategy.

text.p: Unrest in the Balkans has underlined a growing gulf between the "haves" and "have nots" of former communist Europe and questioned one of the main motives behind NATO's planned eastwards expansion, analysts say.

Street protests in Tirana, Sofia, and Belgrade, capitals of three countries with no hope of alliance membership in the foreseeable future, have exposed shortfalls in western thinking over how to spread stability in a volatile region, they say.

"The countries most in need of help and support are those least likely to get it, there is a real disaster in the making here," said Michael Williams of the London-based International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS).

NATO countries plan to name new members from central and eastern Europe at a July summit in Madrid, arguing that -- despite Moscow's virulent opposition -- the alliance's enlargement will help defuse potential regional flashpoints.

But independent analysts and several diplomats say the countries most likely to be admitted in the first wave -- Poland, Hungary, and the Czech Republic -- are relatively stable, increasingly economically viable, and face no threat.

"It is not clear how the admission of these three will help...the problem is those countries that do not get in, countries like the Baltic states that really need security guarantees," said one alliance diplomat.
Critics of enlargement say it could even end up having a destabilising effect, creating a new division in Europe between rich and poor.
"Everyone knows that after this enlargement there will not be another for a long, long time," added Williams.

Supporters say NATO enlargement will give other countries a goal to aim for if they adopt the necessary economic and political reforms and argue the closer they bring the alliance to turbulent areas the greater will be its steadying influence.
"By bringing NATO closer to these areas, it should spread stability. Only time will tell if it will work, but it cannot do any harm," said one alliance official.

Alliance officials say potential membership of NATO has already acted as a catalyst to encourage changes further anchoring the fledgling democracies in the former communist bloc to the rest of democratic Europe.

"It (enlargement) has already encouraged democratic reforms and changes within and among nations," said one senior official, stressing the willingness of candidate countries to settle decades-old border disputes rooted in ethnic rivalries.

Some Western politicians argue that the violent break-up of former Yugoslavia would have been far less likely had the alliance seized the initiative and expanded up to the borders of the Balkans shortly after the collapse of communism.
For the same reason, many are now advocating that Slovenia -- which fulfills many of the conditions for membership -- be admitted in the first round.
"We missed an opportunity in 1990, we must not do it again," said one ambassador to NATO.

Opponents, now increasingly vocal, say there is no evidence a military alliance which could not agree how to deal with the war in Bosnia, Europe's biggest crisis in 50 years, is the best organisation to handle Europe's post-Cold War transformation.

"NATO was created to deter aggression... it did that very well. It is not its job to integrate new democracies, defeat old hatreds, or promote economic recovery," Ian Davidson, a respected British commentator, recently wrote.
Davidson and other critics say the enlargement of the most powerful military alliance ever-assembled cannot take place without alienating Russia.
"Its expansion eastwards must mean a substantial shift in the balance of power with unmistakeable military implications," he wrote in Britain's infuential daily, the Financial Times.
